candidate.answerReason: In a full random ordering of the five chips, all reds are completed before both greens exactly when the last chip is green. Two of the five equally likely last chips are green.

methods.label: Imagine drawing all five chips
methods.explanation:
Imagine continuing to draw after the stopping rule would end the experiment. This gives a random ordering of all five chips without changing which color was completed first.

If the last chip in this full ordering is green, all three reds appear before that chip. At the moment the third red appears, at least one green remains, so the original experiment stops with all three reds drawn.

If the last chip is red, both greens appear before that chip. Thus both greens are drawn before the third red, and the original experiment stops with the greens instead. These two cases cover every ordering.

Each individual chip is equally likely to be last: random drawing without replacement gives no chip a preferred position. Since two of the five chips are green, the requested probability is
\[
\boxed{\frac{2}{5}},
\]
choice \(\text{B}\).
methods.levelReason: The argument uses an elementary equally likely position model and a fraction, without conditional-probability formulas.

Drawing without replacement and interpreting favorable outcomes as a fraction are supporting knowledge. No independence assumption or probability multiplication rule is used.
